concept: Breeze Court Estate: a landward arrival court leads into a tall central great hall framed by two quieter two-level suite wings. The hall opens directly toward a broad ocean terrace and a long water court, while recessed upper galleries, deep roof edges, bronze screens and limestone piers create shade and privacy. Six individually bounded suites occupy the wings: two garden-level ocean suites and four upper suites, including a larger primary allocation. The composition remains low, horizontal and landscape-integrated despite its substantial programme.

alternatives.concept: Terraced linear bar with all suites parallel to the shoreline and living spaces in a projecting central pavilion.
alternatives.tradeoff: Maximizes direct ocean frontage but creates a very long circulation spine and a less protected tropical courtyard.

alternatives.concept: Three detached pavilions linked by covered walkways around a garden court.
alternatives.tradeoff: Offers excellent cross-ventilation and privacy, but weakens the singular estate-scale entrance and increases weather-exposed circulation.

selectionReason: The selected court-and-wings scheme creates the clearest ceremonial sequence from sheltered arrival to ocean view, gives all six suites credible privacy and daylight, supports a direct indoor-outdoor entertainment axis, and allows the central roof to become a memorable silhouette without making the entire estate unnecessarily tall.

site.assumptions: A spacious Saint Lucia waterfront parcel is assumed, with vehicle access from the landward local -Z side and ocean views toward local +Z. Generation must use a single flat ground plane at Y=0, so the stated gentle slope, surveyed shoreline, flood elevation, coastal setbacks and legal boundaries remain unresolved. The estate is organized within an assumed buildable zone of approximately 80 by 95 metres, retaining broad planted side margins.
site.organization: A central north-south ceremonial axis aligns arrival court, entry portal, double-height hall, garden passage, ocean terrace and pool. Two parallel suite wings flank this axis. Service access is reserved along the east side, separated from the western guest garden. Upper suites are reached by a protected internal stair and bridge gallery at the landward end of the great hall.

routes.description: A level, dry ceremonial approach terminates at the sheltered 3.2 metre-wide entrance.
The central living volume opens through a true sill-zero garden door onto the terrace at the same 0.20 metre walking datum.
The terrace abuts the pool coping at its near edge, preserving a continuous dry route around the water.
A protected straight stair rises 4.00 metres to the bridge gallery beneath the elevated central roof.
The bridge turns into the western gallery and enters Suite 3 through its dedicated door.
The same protected gallery serves Suite 4 without crossing another suite.
The eastern gallery branch reaches Suite 5 through a distinct private threshold.
The primary suite is reached through a wider door at the quieter ocean end of the east gallery.
Suite 1 is entered from the western internal side gallery rather than directly from the public terrace.
Suite 2 is entered from the eastern internal side gallery, maintaining privacy from pool circulation.

roofAndSection: The occupied walking datums are 0.20 metres and 4.20 metres. Ground wing walls run from 0.20 to 4.00 metres, with the upper slabs beginning immediately above. Upper suite walls run from 4.20 to 7.40 metres and receive thin 0.30 metre flat roofs at 7.55 metres. The central hall is intentionally taller: its folded mono-pitch roof occupies approximately Y=6.60–7.80 and rises toward the ocean, leaving more than 2.3 metres over the upper bridge. The side roofs remain visually subordinate and extend about 1.2 metres beyond the suite envelopes.
facadeAndClimate: The restrained palette combines pale limestone floors and piers, ivory rendered walls, bronze roof planes and window framing, and warm timber screens. Ocean-facing living openings use 2.9–3.2 metre heads beneath deep roof and pergola shade; bedroom openings are more controlled. The west and east upper elevations receive 0.7 metre-offset vertical timber screens, while the monumental entrance is recessed beneath a 4.5 metre-deep canopy. Openings on opposing garden and ocean elevations provide opportunities for cross-ventilation, but wind, hurricane, corrosion, glare and thermal performance are not simulated.
landscapeAndOutdoorLiving: The outdoor sequence is organized as arrival gardens, shaded threshold, great hall, 10 metre-deep limestone terrace, supported timber pergola and a 24 by 8 metre pool aligned with the ocean view. Broad planted side reserves screen guest and service edges rather than paving the full property. Raised arrival planting masses frame the approach, while the west and east tropical gardens give the suite wings private green outlooks. Planting geometry represents layered landscape zones only, not verified Saint Lucian species or mature canopy.
limitations: This is the required spatial proposal only; no construction operations are included at this stage.
The gentle slope and waterfront terrain cannot be established during new generation, so the proposal uses flat Y=0 ground and does not claim surveyed shoreline, flood elevation or coastal setbacks.
The pool basin, coping and water are representable, but an infinity overflow edge, catch basin, pumps, filtration and hydraulic performance are not represented.

Six suites are individually bounded and accessed as allocated capacity; bathrooms, dressing rooms, kitchen, service rooms, furniture and other interior fit-out remain deferred under the exterior-first scope.
Detailed stair treads, guards, upper gallery balustrades and engineering verification must be resolved during construction.
Planting masses and beds are editable abstractions; species ecology, irrigation, drainage and mature tropical canopy are not simulated.
No structural, hurricane, corrosion, accessibility, life-safety or building-code certification is implied.
The US$25 million figure is treated only as a property-value and design-ambition reference, not as a construction budget, valuation or area formula.
